source.title: Adaptive Probe-based Steering for Robust LLM Jailbreaking
source.authors: Junxi Chen; Junhao Dong; Xiaohua Xie

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table rows are flattened, but the table layout supports the model and metric assignments recorded below.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports harmfulness outcomes for Refusal Direction ablation (RD-A), a contrastive-direction removal baseline, on new fortified models. This is a conceptual test of removal effects, using judge scores rather than the original refusal measure. It also evaluates a different probe-based steering method on a reasoning model.
record.gate_note: Rows cover RD-A in Table 1 and selected RD-A+NA results in Table 3, plus the no-attack and steering results for Qwen3-4B-Thinking in Table 8. The paper's own adaptive-probe attack results in Tables 1–7 and 9 are not rows for V1/V3: they steer toward faithlessness using a separately learned probe, rather than suppressing the specific refusal direction. Probe accuracies used in layer selection, activation norms, and cited results are also not rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs Arditi et al.'s Refusal Direction ablation (RD-A) as a baseline on 12 defense-fortified LLMs, 7 general-purpose LLMs and 3 AdaSteer LLMs, scoring harmful-prompt outputs with three judges. These results bear on V1 (ablation removes refusal) in a new setting: fortified models, judged by harmfulness rather than refusal rate. A within-family comparison (Mistral-7B-Instruct vs its SU/RB/CB versions) bears on V7. The paper's own method is a separately learned, iteratively retrained per-layer probe direction, not the difference-in-means direction, so its results (including the reasoning-model Table 8) do not test V1 or V8.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that adaptive retraining (model extraction) and activation-statistics-based strength selection make probe-based steering a more effective and robust jailbreak. It raises fortified models' average harmfulness from 6% to 70% and also breaks reasoning and multimodal models. They add that the Refusal Direction baseline is second best on average but often fails to find a direction because its filtering is not robust.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses contrastive activations and steers hidden states, but its proposed method trains probe directions using judge-annotated activations and iterative retraining rather than relying only on a difference-in-means direction. RD-A is included as an ablation baseline; the main method steers toward faithlessness rather than ablating the refusal direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports model- and judge-dependent outcomes, unavailable RD directions on some models, and effects of prompt-set size in Table 3. It also reports sensitivity to SRF thresholds, token positions, steering strength, and judges for its own method; those outcomes are not rows for the refusal-direction versions catalogued here.

fits_no_version.finding: An adaptively retrained per-layer linear probe, steered at all positions, raises harmfulness to 0.67–0.97 on reasoning model Qwen3-4B-Thinking (from 0.03–0.19). Across 12 fortified models it reaches an average of 0.70.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A learned (non-difference-in-means) linear steering direction removes refusal even in fortified and reasoning models where the DIM direction fails.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors argue that harmful-minus-harmless contrast directions carry coupled concepts (e.g. ethical vs unethical, cake vs bomb). They show that adding 871 contrast pairs barely helps (Fig. 1a, Sec 3.3.1, Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Difference-in-means refusal directions from harmful/harmless prompts are confounded with other content directions.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: Table 1 reports no no-attack baseline for RD-A, and the outcomes are judge harmfulness scores rather than direct refusal rates. No capability-preservation result is reported for RD-A. Some models have no available RD direction. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the table scores. Table 3 results were only partly extracted due to the 60-row limit.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 RD-A+NA results for Mistral-RB, Llama3-LAT, Llama3-TAR, Llama3-CB, R2D2, and Llama3-DeRTA were left out to stay within 60 rows; Table 3. Other RD-A+NA results for the selected models were retained when they showed unavailable directions or model-specific outcomes. Results for the paper's own method and other steering baselines were left out because they do not test the specific refusal-direction ablation claims.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts (used only inside RD's filter, not reported). Capability preservation under RD-A. Refusal rate itself: only judge harmfulness scores are reported.
No weight-edit or abliterated release is evaluated.
No analysis of whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction. No training against its ablation.
No affine, cone or multi-direction test; only an argument about coupled concepts in contrast prompts.
No transfer of directions across languages or model variants.
Only the Mistral-family contrast is informative. When refusal training happens (base vs instruct, timing) is not tested.
RD-A is not run on any reasoning model. Table 8 uses only the paper's probe steering.

missing.what: RD-C (refusal-direction constant-strength steering) harmfulness on all 12 fortified models, e.g. Llama3-CB 0.28/0.38/0.35 and Mistral-RB 0.23/0.25/0.34

RD-A and RD-C on 7 general-purpose models. RD-A gives Mistral-7B-Instruct 0.69/0.79/0.92 and Gemma-2-9b-it 0.66/0.71/0.85. No direction is found on Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7b and Vicuna-7b.
RD-A on AdaSteer models: Gemma-2-9b-AdaSteer 0.33/0.35/0.42; no direction on the Llama-3.1 and Qwen2.5 versions
Unattacked baseline for fortified models (average harmfulness 6%)
Explanation that RD fails because its filter rejects all candidates; with 871 pairs RD also fails on Llama3-TAR

record.verdict_notes: RD-A is a baseline run with the original direction-selection filter, 100 contrast pairs and a 4:1 split. Outcomes are judge harmfulness scores (SRF/HB/SR), which reward helpful harmful content. A non-refusing but incoherent output therefore scores low, so absent states cannot fully separate 'refusal intact' from 'refusal removed but output degraded'. V3 was removed from all rows because nothing tests jailbreak mechanism or training against ablation. V8 was removed because Table 8 uses only the paper's probe method. The tranche is T3 rather than T2: RD-A uses the original method, but on new defended models with a different measure.

versions.untested_parts: The RD-A ablation results bear on removal and harmful compliance, but the study does not test adding the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests, nor does it test preservation of general capabilities under that ablation. It does not isolate the difference-in-means recipe as the sole direction-finding method.
No abliteration or other practical weight edit is evaluated.
RD-A removal is evaluated as a contrastive-steering baseline, but the study does not test training against the ablation to add robustness.
The paper discusses coupled concepts in contrastive prompts, but does not test affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal.
No separate encoding of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is tested.
Models are evaluated with their own steering directions; no cross-language or cross-model direction transfer is tested.
The study compares models with different defenses but does not test how refusal-training choices determine whether a removable direction exists.
The study tests probe-based steering on Qwen3-4B-Thinking, not the difference-in-means direction and ablation/addition intervention specified by V1. Only one reasoning model is tested.
